changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
changes.change: For merchants whose biggest risk is a live peak event, such as ticketing on-sales, lead with people, not tiers: 'A name, not a queue.' Introduce by name the people who will run the account, give the direct line they will answer, and lay out the escalation path, all before the deciding meeting. Keep response-time SLAs as supporting detail.
changes.why: When the rep walked the COO through 'The tiers, the response times,' she dismissed it as 'a queue with a faster timer,' while the competitor won by showing up 'with the people who'd actually be on the account.'

changes.change: For peak-event merchants, add a written on-sale or peak-event plan as a standard deal asset, introduced with the buyer's own line: 'I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down.' The plan should state who is watching during the event, who the customer calls, and what happens in the first minutes of a live failure. Present it to the operations owner, not only to the technical team.
changes.why: The decider asked to see 'on paper, what we do on an on-sale morning,' and the rep had to admit 'We don't have that as a thing,' after a failure that started 'about four minutes in.'

changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
changes.change: For peak-event buyers, replace the logo slide with a reference customer, ideally in ticketing, who will speak directly about who picked up during their own big on-sale.
changes.why: The rep said 'I had logos. I didn't have a person.' Logos could not answer a buyer who was asking for 'Someone who picks up.'
